title: Israel's story, looking back
hookLine: from Jericho to the return: a faithful God, an up-and-down people
tomorrow: what's worth saying out loud, even with stones flying?

cards: Graduation day: parents in the bleachers crying, kids on the floor cheering, all of it at once. The Bible has a moment like that.
After exile, some of the people come home to a ruined Jerusalem and lay the foundation of a new temple. The younger ones shout for joy. The old ones, who remember the first temple, weep out loud.
And Ezra says “the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people.”

teach.b: That mixed sound is the whole story, looking back. These books are first the story of the Jewish people, and Christians read them as scripture too. And they're honest.
They don't polish their heroes. Walls fall at Jericho. Then the judges, and a blunt verdict: “every man did that which was right in his own eyes.”
David dances before the LORD, and takes another man's wife. Solomon builds the temple, and his heart turns after other gods.
Good kings, bad kings, prophets calling the people home. Then Jerusalem falls.

teach.h: NEW EVERY MORNING, IN THE RUINS.
teach.b: Out of the ruins comes a book of grief, Lamentations, and in it: “his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.”

teach.h: A LOW POINT ISN'T THE LAST CHAPTER.
teach.b: Faithfulness, named from inside the rubble. So what does this story give someone in a bad week? Not a promise that the ups and downs stop.
A people up and down, like any people, and a God the text keeps calling faithful through all of it. In this story, a low point isn't the last chapter, and it isn't proof that God has let go.

how: Jews read these books as their own history and scripture. In churches, passages from Joshua, the books of Kings, Lamentations and Ezra come up among the Old Testament readings, and some congregations sing a hymn built on 'great is thy faithfulness.'

o: a list of laws for the Temple's priests
a people's ups and downs, and a God called faithful
a single victory story of one king's conquests

games.q: ups and downs — tap the pairs.

s: the Bible presents its heroes as flawless role models
it shows David's and Solomon's failures plainly.
Lamentations names God's faithfulness while Jerusalem lies in ruins
great is thy faithfulness, written in grief.
at the new temple's foundation, everyone cheered
the old wept aloud, the young shouted for joy, and you couldn't tell the sounds apart.

games.q: your older brother failed a class he needed and says he's clearly not cut out for anything. what does Israel's story offer him?
o: one bad chapter shows he should change plans for good.
a low point isn't the last chapter; the story keeps going.
pretend it didn't happen and move straight on.
games.why: the books record failures honestly and keep going: exile, then return. the text keeps naming faithfulness through the lows.

practice: On any scrap of paper, draw one line for your year: up for the high points, down for the low ones, flat for the long middle. Mark one low spot with a small dot, and beside it write who or what held you there.
If you pray, rest on the words from Lamentations: great is thy faithfulness.

wordCard.voice: Israel's story. From Jericho to the return: an honest record of a people's ups and downs, and of a faithfulness the text keeps naming.

orig.note: Hebrew: faithfulness, steadiness. 'great is thy faithfulness' in Lamentations 3:23 uses this word.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: still faithful, said from inside the ruins. Day seventeen-sixty-nine, ups and downs and all.
